items.stem: State what is meant by 'flowchart'.
items.answer: A diagram that represents an algorithm using standard symbols connected by flow lines.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A diagram that represents an algorithm using standard symbols connected by flow lines. [2]

items.stem: Explain why the order of instructions in an algorithm matters.
items.answer: Instructions are carried out in sequence; doing them in a different order can give a different or wrong result, e.g. outputting a total before adding the last value.
items.markingKey: 1 mark sequence; 1 mark example of wrong result. [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage of representing an algorithm as a flowchart.
items.answer: It shows the flow of control visually, so decisions and loops are easy to follow, and it is independent of any programming language.
items.markingKey: 1 mark visual flow; 1 mark easy to follow/language independent. [2]

items.stem: Students at Palm Grove Hotel in Auckland are learning to show algorithms as flowcharts. Draw the flowchart symbol used for a decision and state what it contains.
items.answer: A diamond containing a question/condition with Yes and No exits.
items.markingKey: 1 mark diamond; 1 mark question with two exits. [2]

items.stem: Students at Palm Grove Hotel in Lima are learning to show algorithms as flowcharts. (a) State which symbol would be used for "OUTPUT Bonus" and for "Bonus ← Salary * 0.05". (b) Describe how a loop is shown on a flowchart.
items.answer: (a) Parallelogram (input/output); rectangle (process). (b) A decision box tests a condition; a flow line from one exit returns to an earlier point; the other exit continues.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. [2] (b) 1 mark decision; 1 mark flow line back. [2]

items.stem: Yusuf at TransGlobal Logistics in Lagos is drawing a flowchart for a program that calculates staff bonuses. Discuss the use of flowcharts rather than pseudocode to plan programs at TransGlobal Logistics.
items.answer: Points for: visual and easy for non-programmers; shows decisions and loops clearly; language independent. Points against / limitations: large algorithms become very big and hard to edit; time-consuming to draw; pseudocode is closer to real code. Conclusion: flowcharts suit small algorithms and communication with non-programmers; pseudocode suits larger ones.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Against: large algorithms become very big and hard to edit; time-consuming to draw; pseudocode is closer to real code. Conclusion may argue: flowcharts suit small algorithms and communication with non-programmers; pseudocode suits larger ones. [4]

items.stem: Explain what is meant by the term 'decision symbol'.

items.stem: Explain why a decision symbol is needed to create a loop in a flowchart.

items.stem: Define the term 'selection'.
items.answer: A construct in which a condition is tested and different instructions are carried out depending on the result, e.g. IF ... THEN ... ELSE or CASE.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a WHILE loop and a REPEAT ... UNTIL loop.
items.answer: WHILE tests its condition before each iteration, so it may run zero times; REPEAT tests at the end, so it always runs at least once.
items.markingKey: 1 mark WHILE pre-condition/may not run; 1 mark REPEAT post-condition/at least once. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a FOR loop is not suitable for validating an input until it is correct.

items.stem: Daniel is designing an algorithm for Horizon Travel in Istanbul that reads daily temperatures and reports statistics. Discuss the choice of loop types in the algorithm for Horizon Travel.
items.answer: Points for: FOR loops are simple when counts are known; condition-controlled loops handle unknown amounts of data and validation. Points against / limitations: wrong choice can cause loops that run too many or too few times or never end; REPEAT always runs once even when no data exists. Conclusion: the loop should match whether the number of iterations is known in advance.
